extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers, and psychologists studying creativity and the process of mathematical discovery
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and prescriptive account of the psychological stages, habits, and conditions that foster mathematical discovery, including a questionnaire of working methods and illustrative historical examples (Poincaré, Gauss, Einstein, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of the inventive process (preparation, incubation, illumination, verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention typically proceeds through stages: a preparation stage of deliberate work, an incubation (unconscious) period where ideas ferment, an illumination (sudden insight) when the solution appears, and later conscious work to verify and elaborate the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multi-stage model (adopted from Poincaré and Wallas) is illustrated repeatedly (Poincaré's sleeping/night bus/walking examples). The author emphasizes that after an illumination the conscious stage of verification and extension is essential; sudden insight is not the final product but a beginning that must be checked and developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the unconscious (incubation) in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior unconscious work is necessary for many sudden enlightenments: an idea appearing as if out of nowhere is the manifestation of previous, unperceived mental processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard (following Poincaré) argues that unconsciousness is manifold and synthetic, able to combine many elements simultaneously. Examples: Poincaré's fuchsian functions, Gauss's arithmetic theorem, Mozart's musical composition. The unconscious performs a combinatory synthesis that the narrow conscious mind cannot, so incubation is a productive phase rather than mere absence of activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chance is not a sufficient explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure chance (randomness) cannot adequately explain inventive insight; chance may act but only in interaction with prior preparation and the inventor's unconscious work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book criticizes theories (Nicolle, Souriau in extreme form) that attribute discovery to accident alone. Hadamard distinguishes external chance (experimental accidents) from psychological chance (fortuitous mental events) and insists that psychological chance only becomes intelligible given antecedent work and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of illumination (sudden solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illuminations tend to be sudden, brief, and accompanied by immediate certainty — the solution 'comes' whole and without intermediate conscious steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré's accounts (idea while boarding omnibus, idea while walking on bluff) exemplify the brevity and certainty of illumination. Similar phenomena are reported by Gauss, Helmholtz, Mozart (creative flash), and many respondents to historical questionnaires. The phenomenon is distinct from dreaming; often solutions appear upon abrupt awakening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation: deep conscious study and problem immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough prior work—intensive study, repeated attempts, and immersion in the problem domain—prepares the unconscious to synthesize solutions during incubation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard follows Poincaré in stressing that the unconscious work presupposes long, conscious preparation. The text discusses differences between mathematicians who study predecessors intensively and those who prefer to 'rediscover' by thought; both approaches have been observed. Preparation includes mastering antecedent results, methods, and analogies that feed unconscious combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate verification and elaboration after insight
rubrics_metrics.description: After a sudden intuition arises, the discoverer must subject it to rigorous conscious scrutiny, proof, and refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré verified the ideas he had in sudden insight when he returned to study them. Hadamard emphasizes that invention is incomplete until it is consciously elaborated and reduced to formal proof or extended into a usable theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatory play and internal signs/images (thought elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive thought often consists of a combinatory play of signs or mental images (visual, muscular, etc.) which are manipulated before they are expressed in words; words and formal signs are secondary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Einstein's testimonial (Appendix II) is quoted: his thought elements are 'certain signs and more or less clear images' (visual and muscular), and words only intervene at a later stage. This 'play' is the essential feature of productive thought prior to logical construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe-consciousness / 'ante-chamber' of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a near-conscious fringe (ante-chamber) holding many allied ideas ready to be summoned into full consciousness in sequence; this borderline layer facilitates the flow from unconscious to conscious thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard cites Galton's 'ante-chamber' metaphor and Galton/Wallace/Gestalt ideas: a narrow conscious 'presence-chamber' and a surrounding antechamber of ideas that the mind can draw upon relatively mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and synthetic capability of the unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The unconscious can hold and process multiple elements simultaneously (a manifold), enabling synthetic operations (e.g., face recognition as synthesis of many features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multiplicity contrasts with the unity and narrowness of conscious attention; the unconscious's capacity to combine many items is central to its role in generating novel syntheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of method: specialize-first vs generalize-first
rubrics_metrics.description: Two opposing research heuristics: begin with special cases and generalize progressively, or attempt a broad/general study first and then examine specific cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The questionnaire (Appendix I) explicitly asks which method mathematicians prefer. Hadamard discusses that different problems may require different approaches and that personal style matters; both methods are used by successful workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pause/temporary abandonment (incubation technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate interruption—leaving a problem aside for a time—can foster incubation and lead to later breakthroughs when unconscious recombination occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard and many respondents (and Poincaré) recommend letting the mind 'sleep on it' or abandoning a problem temporarily and then resuming it; this is a pragmatic tactic for stimulating unconscious processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording vs delaying formal write-up (immediate note-taking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to write down a spontaneously arisen discovery immediately or to collect impressions/notes and do redaction later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix I asks whether one writes down parts immediately upon discovery or lets conclusions accumulate in notes and begins formal drafting only when content is substantial. Guidance: many practitioners adopt the habit most compatible with their workflow; important to capture fleeting insights in some form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity of work and minimum effective practice (small daily study)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular, sustained practice (even short amounts daily) is recommended for profitable study of mathematical branches; specify a minimum time commitment (questionnaire suggests at least one hour daily if possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix I asks the minimum number of hours per day/week/year a mathematician with other demands should devote. Hadamard recommends habitual study, often favoring small but regular daily engagement over sporadic long sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hygiene: sleep, diet, stimulants, and physical exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical health factors (sleep amount, diet/regular meals, stimulants like coffee/tobacco/alcohol, and exercise) materially affect the quality and quantity of mathematical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The questionnaire requests specifics: normal sleep amount, effects of stimulants/sedatives, whether vacations are used for study or rest, and whether exercise/physical occupations interrupt or aid work. Hadamard treats these as significant determinants of creative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and psychological state (periods of exaltation and depression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions and mood states (exaltation, depression) influence creative production, possibly favoring different kinds of mental creation; periods of high activity can be followed by inactivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard cites Paul Valéry and others noting that powerful emotions can favor mathematical as well as poetic invention. The questionnaire asks whether respondents experience alternating periods of inspiration and incapacity and whether such cycles are regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of external conditions (noise, meteorological factors, place)
rubrics_metrics.description: External environmental conditions—noise, weather, season, working location—can appreciably influence one's ability to work productively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix I and the text ask whether noises disturb, whether one can think while walking or on a train, whether meteorological conditions affect work, and whether one prefers to work on blackboard or paper; answers are considered informative for optimizing working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value (and study) of failures as well as successes
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the genesis of failures and the reasons for non-success is at least as important as recording successes; failures provide critical information about methods and pitfalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard criticizes early questionnaires for asking mainly about successes; he urges collecting reasons for failures (but notes that many respondents hesitate to report failures). Studying failures helps identify methodological issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of mathematical minds (multiple cognitive types)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not one single 'mathematical aptitude' or mind type; several distinct kinds of mathematical minds exist and differ significantly in how they think and discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard emphasizes that mathematical creativity connects to general intelligence but is composite; historical and questionnaire evidence suggests different practitioners rely on varying mixtures of intuition, imagery, logic, and representational modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing invention to reflex or purely peripheral mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatic or reflex explanations (e.g., reflex motions, phrenological bumps) are inadequate to account for complex acts of invention or automatic writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard considers phenomena like automatic writing and shows they cannot be explained away as mere peripheral reflexes; complex cognitive centers and unconscious processes are implicated rather than simple reflex arcs or phrenological localizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective vs introspective methods for studying invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methodological approaches exist for studying invention: introspective (subjective reports, self-observation) and objective (external observation, questionnaires, experimental measures); each has strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard defends use of introspection for investigating inventive processes (given his competence) but recognizes experimental/behaviorist critiques. He recommends combining methods where possible, noting limitations (e.g., rarity of exceptional inventive events makes statistical objective study difficult).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between invention and redaction (different habits required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive activity (finding new results) and redaction (writing them up) are distinct tasks and may require different mental modes and habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix I asks whether one distinguishes between invention and redacting in method. Hadamard notes that some habits suitable for discovery (e.g., associative play) differ from those suitable for formal exposition and proof-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal representational modality matters (visual, motor, auditory imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of internal representations used in thought (visual, motor, auditory, or mixed) significantly shapes the way a mathematician thinks and discovers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 30 and Einstein's reply (Appendix II) underline that many mathematicians use visual and muscular images; words appear at a secondary stage. Appendix I solicits data on whether mental pictures and internal word-forms occur in full consciousness or the fringe, and whether arguments appear as geometric images or verbal chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of analogy and cross-disciplinary inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies to other fields (physics, biology, geometry, arts) can trigger insights and provide fruitful directions for mathematical invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard gives historical examples (Fermat, Newton/Leibniz development, calculus antecedents) and comments that biology, music, or arts sometimes aid mathematicians. The questionnaire explores interests in non-mathematical sciences and their possible influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social, historical, and hereditary influences on invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Social context, historical milieu, and hereditary background likely influence the development and directions of invention, though mechanisms are often obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hadamard discusses—cautiously—the roles of heredity (families of mathematicians), social conditions (Renaissance Italy producing many exceptional minds), and historical parallels; he calls for careful individual studies rather than broad speculative claims.
